title: The Student Revolt in France Spreads
content:
from the 

CrimethInc. 

collective, 21/10/2026







Moving Forward with Rage and Solidarity




October 17 marked one of the fiercest days of mass protest in recent French history. Scenes of ferocious resistance unfolded throughout the day, not only in Paris but in 

Bordeaux

, 

Dijon

, 

Marseille

, 

Nancy

, and dozens of other cities across the country. Some observers have described the day’s events as 

more explosive

 than the 

Yellow Vest movement

 of 2018-19—and the rebellion shows no sign of slowing.




How did we get here? Courageous high school students 

have been protesting for weeks

 against abominable conditions in schools, the rise of the extreme right, and the bleak prospects they face in a world dominated by technocrats and tech barons. Alongside growing anti-government protests from 

Albania

, 

Italy

, 

Spain

, and beyond in recent days, the French student rebellions may herald the emergence of a new wave of global struggle.




In this article, our correspondent from Paris explains the context behind the youth rebellion, tracks the movement’s growth over the two weeks leading up to October 17 and the government’s failed attempts to repress or to pacify it, and clarifies the stakes moving forward.




Stay tuned for a full report on the uprising of October 17 and the ongoing rebellions across France and beyond.







Thousands gather to protest police violence and support the students in revolt (Nantes, October 6, 2026)







This update on the student unrest in France picks up where we ended 

our previous report

, on the eve of the national call to take the streets on October 6, 2026.




The stakes were high on this crucial day of action. It was critical to show massive solidarity with the high school students fighting like hell against the empty future looming on their horizon. The day presented an ideal opportunity to expand the scope of the current movement by joining forces to resist the authoritarian state power that has been growing stronger every day.




The following article provides further context and analysis to understand the current situation in France, along with reports on what went down in the streets over these last rebellious weeks.




Background: The 

Banlieues

 and the Enemy Within




When governments or powerful institutions feel threatened, they often strive to reaffirm their authority by inventing scapegoats to hold responsible for all supposed misfortunes. By invoking the menace of an “enemy within,” politicians can shift blame for systemic problems that have resulted from their own actions onto a specific category of individuals. In France, the most common targets are the residents of the 

banlieues

, the impoverished suburbs on the outskirts of Paris and other cities.




At the beginning of the student blockades, the movement remained limited to a handful of high schools in these Parisian suburbs. In response, President Emmanuel Macron and his ministers decided to react quickly and do everything in their power to silence this emerging wave of youth protest. Due to the location of the first blockades, authorities believed that they could act more freely and repress the unrest with impunity, since these specific territories have been targeted for generations by all government administrations across political lines.




The condition of the 

banlieues

, which remain populated by descendants of the French Empire’s colonized subjects, reflects France’s ongoing role as a 

neocolonial power

 that continues to exploit African territories. Consider the disastrous 

oil project

 in Uganda orchestrated by the France-based multinational company TotalEnergies, or the 

corruption case

 involving the French far-right business tycoon Vincent Bolloré and his bribery and money laundering schemes across West African ports.




French governments and corporations have no scruples about extracting enormous wealth from African countries. This neocolonial pillaging fuels France’s position as the 

seventh richest country

 in the world today, according to the IMF. Yet despite these astronomical profits, the nation refuses to address the problems facing its post-colonial population and their descendants within its national territory.




At the twilight of France’s colonial empire, decades of occupation and racist violence had created political and economic instability across northern and western Africa. As a result, waves of migrants began leaving their countries to come to France for work in the 1950s. Upon arriving, they continued to face systemic colonial racism, relegated to the economic margins and second-class citizenship. This cheap workforce ended up gathering on the outskirts of major cities, living in makeshift neighborhoods and slums like those of 

Nanterre

 on the western edges of Paris.




Shantytown in the Parisian suburb of Nanterre in the 1960s




Over the following decades, urban development projects replaced these slums with massive apartment blocks into which immigrant families and low-income workers were relocated. Today, these areas are known as the 

banlieues

 (the suburbs). In mainstream French political discourse, authorities and journalists invoke the 

banlieues

 as a derogatory term that embodies all the supposed flaws of our modern society.




The 

banlieues

 also offer areas of experimentation for law enforcement. Politicians ranging from moderate to reactionary have long considered these suburbs “lawless areas” whose young residents pose a threat to the ruling order. In response, the French state consistently harasses and represses these populations to instill fear and obedience and to force them to adapt to its laws. This targeted violence reproduces old colonial strategies within the territory of the nation. For example, the “state of emergency,” developed as legal tool in former French colonies for crowd control, was first used within the borders of France in the 

banlieues

.




Past governments pushed law enforcement to increase the pressure in the suburbs, invoking the “war on drugs” and defense of their sacrosanct “democracy.” They invested in new weapons and equipment, which specific police units experimented with freely in the streets of the 

banlieues

 to test their usefulness in repressing popular mobilization. These racist police forces operate with impunity in these territories and consider every person they encounter a potential threat. As a result, numerous young people of color have been abused, injured, or killed at the hands of police, such as Zyed Benna and Bouna Traore in 

2005

, Adama Traoré in 

2016

, and more recently, Nahel Merzouk in 

2023

.




In the face of such contemptuous violence from the French state and its armed henchmen, it is inevitable that people would organize on a grassroot level to defend themselves and counterattack against these intolerable conditions. It is simply a question of dignity and survival. Historically, the 

banlieues

 have been the settings of intense riots and confrontations with police forces, often leading to massive property destruction and arsons.




In this context, it is not a coincidence that the student blockades first emerged in these suburbs, nor that the government decided without hesitation to send in heavily equipped police forces to repress them. This response is only a logical extension of the long legacy of colonial racism directed against part of the population. The French state continues to consider working-class people and the children of immigrants as the biggest threat to its stability. Therefore, to maintain its crumbling power structure by any means necessary, its solution is to constantly terrorize these youths to contain their rebellious energy.




The repressive technologies used by police against students and protesters today were tested out on the populations of the 

banlieues

 (Lyon, October 6, 2026)




Keeping the Rage Alive




After more than a week of intense confrontations and blockades throughout France, it became clear that curbing the ungovernable student movement had become the number one priority of the current ruling order.




Nevertheless, the movement refused to be intimidated by the brutal repression implemented by authorities. Instead, it paid tribute in its own way to the 

Yellow Vest

 unrest that began in 2018 by rebranding its own key days of actions as “Acts.” This framework of successive mobilizations, each building on the last, maintained the pressure on politicians and law enforcement by providing regular opportunities to take the streets in massive demonstrations on a national scale.




While these national days of action appeared once or twice per week, this doesn’t mean that nothing happened the rest of the week. On the contrary, multiple forms of action—blockades, sit-ins, direct confrontations with police forces, property destruction, arsons, and more—continued to take place daily across multiple cities throughout France. This plurality of tactics, combined with the courage and determination of numerous teenagers throughout the past weeks, has enabled the unrest to last this long.




Clouds of tear gas in Rennes (October 6, 2026)




Act III: October 6, 2026




On the morning of Tuesday, October 6, students gathered in front of their high schools and universities to block access. This time, due to the state’s escalation of violence against the youth demonstrations over the previous days, parents and teachers decided to join the students and assembled with them in front of schools. Through their presence, they hoped to prevent intensifying repression from police forces.




For the most part, their strategy appears to have worked. Reports from different blockades during the morning mentioned that on the whole, tensions were not as high as on previous days. Nevertheless, some locations saw police officers attempting to break through the lines of some parents and teachers who were protecting students or using pepper-spray to disperse protesters.




It is difficult to confirm whether the less brutal state response that morning resulted from police reluctance due to the presence of adults among students, or from specific orders coming from government officials. After the increasing number of injuries inflicted on students over the preceding days, the government may have instructed its armed forces to be more careful while dealing with student blockades, especially with parents and teachers joining them.




Parents and teachers on the front line to defend their children and students (Bordeaux, October 6, 2026)




While parents and teachers joining their students on the front lines during these morning actions may have discouraged a more violent response from the state, their presence in the blockades may also have helped authorities to regain some partial control in the streets. The presence of such authority figures can play a role in discouraging rebellious behavior among young people. In the days to come, the success of the unrest may depend in part on whether students can receive support from adults while maintaining their own autonomy and momentum.




That same morning, as the first demonstrations were taking place in Lille, Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, Nantes, and other cities, some university students blocked their campuses to join the movement. Around noon, as people converged at the Place de la République for the Paris demonstration, authorities announced that 891 of the country’s 3700 high schools were either partially or completely closed, including 250 just in the Paris region. Contrary to the official announcements made by the government, the movement was gaining rather than losing momentum.




The Paris demonstration was scheduled to depart from Place de la République in the direction of Place de la Nation. The 3.3-kilometer pathway connecting these two major squares in eastern Paris has frequently been the scene of social movement marches and intense clashes with police forces. This time, however, we learned beforehand that police units had received orders to keep their distance from demonstrators and to not be “visible” to prevent escalating tensions. The government appeared to have adapted its law enforcement strategy for the day in response to mounting criticisms of its repression of the students since the beginning of the movement.




Before the official departure time of the procession, the square was already so packed that thousands of demonstrators had begun walking down the boulevard towards La Nation to make space for more people to join. The flow of individuals passing through Place de la République seemed endless. Massive numbers of high school and university students, teachers and other educational workers were joined by leftist organizations, trade unions, and other supporters, as well as some radicals and anarchists. The feeling among the crowds was festive, impassioned, and full of determination.




As the crowd approached Place de la Nation, the atmosphere gradually changed. Police units in riot gear were blocking adjacent streets preventing anyone from entering or exiting the procession. Marchers erected a makeshift barricade and set it ablaze in the middle of the boulevard, while several targets had their front windows smashed and their offices ransacked. After weeks of brutal attacks on the protesting students, this escalation of tactics reflected the justified rage and desire to take the offensive that many demonstrators felt.




At this point, intense confrontations with police forces began at Place de la Nation. Riot police and 

BRAV-M special units

 encountered showers of stones and projectiles thrown by courageous rioters, while the rest of the crowd of protesters that did not physically take part showed their support by chanting the classic “

Tout le monde déteste la police

” (“Everyone hates the police”) and shouting, “

ACAB

”.




Police forces used tear gas, stun grenades and rubber bullets to attempt to disperse the thick crowds entering La Nation. But people stayed, continuing to demonstrate and hanging out amid the joyful chaos. At times, officers charged demonstrators in order to snatch and arrest specific individuals, while determined individuals counterattacked them head-on and without respite. The solidarity experienced during these moments was a breath of fresh air among the thick clouds of tear gas.




At the end of the day, despite the false reassurances of the authorities in the mainstream media, the third national day of action was a clear victory for the movement. The objective of gathering masses of people in the streets to join forces with the students had been achieved. According to unions and organizations, at least 450,000 demonstrators participated across France, around one fourth in Paris. As usual, authorities announced much 

lower numbers

, estimating around 250,000 total demonstrators. Moreover, to reassure the nation of its control over the situation, the government’s Ministry of the Interior announced that 488 individuals had been arrested during the day, raising the total of arrests since the beginning of the movement to an unprecedented number of 6547.




These figures illustrate the escalation of authoritarian law enforcement doctrine in France. By comparison, during the first 26 days of the Yellow Vest movement, French police recorded around 12,000 arrests, an average of 460 each day. Eight years later, these 

figures

 have been dramatically surpassed. As of October 6, 2026, approximately 935 arrests had taken place every single day since the beginning of the movement.




Despite these disturbing figures reflecting growing mass arrests, the student movement did not back down. Their persistence in the streets shows their determination to continue fighting, not only to improve the 

conditions in their schools

 but to challenge the living hell the French authorities are drawing tighter around us every day.




Students building a barricade in front of their high school (Paris, October 8, 2026)




Act IV: October 8, 2026




Two days after this impressive mobilization in the streets, student unions issued another call for mass convergence in the streets to maintain pressure on the government. As they had done for nearly two weeks, students from all over the country woke up early to meet in front of their schools, build makeshift barricades, and block the main entrances.




By 8:00 am, hundreds of high schools remained blocked in different cities. In the Paris region alone, about 145 schools were either closed, blocked or experiencing some sort of disruption. The Ministry of Education announced that 224 schools were completely closed and 151 partially closed. Authorities used these figures to once again claim that the movement was losing momentum, since “94% of high schools in France were completely or partially open” on this Thursday morning.




On this new day of action, a demonstration was scheduled to take place in Paris during the afternoon. However, the city’s Police Prefecture refused to approve the initial route requested by student unions. Instead, authorities only allowed students and protesters to converge and gather at Place de la Bastille, an ideal location for 

kettling

 large crowds of individuals by closing all access to the square.




Nevertheless, an estimated 

25,000 students and other demonstrators

 gathered at La Bastille, while demonstrations also took place in Lille, Lyon, Marseille, Nantes, Rennes, Toulon, and other cities.




After several uneventful hours in the plaza, confusion began to spread among demonstrators, as no one knew where to leave the demonstration with police units holding their lines in front of every potential exit. The crowd simmered as people moved from one street to another seeking a way to escape from this trap.




Unsurprisingly, this stressful situation led to clashes with law enforcement. As the sun set, tensions between protesters and police escalated. To “clear the square,” police forces carried out repeated violent charges and shot tear gas canisters, rubber bullets, and sting ball grenades at demonstrators. Courageous rioters answered by shooting fireworks and throwing paving stones, glass bottles, and other projectiles. Authorities struggling to disperse the remaining protesters deployed a water cannon. Reports suggested that several individuals were injured in the clashes that afternoon. While the last groups of demonstrators were still resisting police attacks at La Bastille and in the nearby streets, other demonstrators attempted to regroup at Place de la Nation, but were rapidly surrounded by officers.




Riot police units attempt to clear out 

La Bastille

 (Paris, October 8, 2026)




At the end of the day, the government 

announced

 that 71,500 people had participated in the afternoon demonstrations across the country, including 25,000 in Paris. 55,000 took part in actions in front of high schools, of whom only some joined the afternoon processions and gatherings. Officials reported 504 arrests on October 8.




But government statistics should be interpreted with extreme caution. For example, authorities claimed that since the beginning of the movement on September 17, 215 students, 85 teachers and education staff members, and 800 police officers had been injured. These figures seem dubious, given the unlikelihood that heavily equipped police officers would receive injuries at far higher rates than mostly unarmed high school students and other protesters. As always during protest movements, the war of numbers offers authorities a useful tool to build their narrative and justify their actions.




Repressions and Concessions: The State Tries to Undermine Solidarity




In the face of this increasing wave of solidarity with students and boiling anger against government inaction and 

police violence

, the Macron administration desperately attempted to keep up appearances while deploying strategies to divide the movement and regain control.




During a speech to the National Assembly on October 6, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu reiterated the need to deploy large numbers of law enforcement officers in the streets to counter the “violence” spread by the student movement. This shows the government’s willingness to legitimize the use of brutal force against the nation’s teenagers without second-guessing its policies or even admitting the existence of “police violence”.




All sorts of media outlets have widely reported how students have been insulted, assaulted, brutalized, and injured by police forces since the beginning of the movement. In response, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez 

stated

 that law enforcement actions have been carried out with “the utmost proportionality” and that he refused to apologize for any of the state’s actions since the emergence of the movement.




Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who is in charge of the management of public order in response to the students protest movement (Paris, October 7, 2026)




In the same breath, without a hint of shame for its glaring hypocrisy, the government also 

announced

 that the use of stun grenades by police against the student movement would be suspended until further notice, following the tragic 

loss of a hand by young protestor

 on October 5. Such decisions refute the government’s own narrative of “proportionality,” as they are well aware that they are targeting teenagers with military weapons intended to cause physical or mental injury, if not death. This hypocrisy, while not surprising, remains infuriating.




Hoping to divert attention from the protestors’ demands, the government also announced its decision to accelerate discussions regarding the voting of a bill named “

casseurs-payeurs

.” This new repressive measure was first proposed last May in the aftermath of the riots and lootings that followed the victory of the PSG (the Parisian football team) during the final game of the Champions League. Its aim is simple: to make the families of suspected rioters pay for damages they allegedly caused. This law, a favorite proposal of the extreme right for years, would force any individual who knowingly took part in a group that committed violence, theft, or damage to pay up to 10,000€ [over $11,000] each towards repairs.




But the law goes beyond restitution into criminalizing participation in nearly any public resistance. Authorities will not have to prove that a specific individual broke anything; simply belonging to a group of “rioters” will suffice to find someone guilty. Any time a person decides to remain in the streets after police ordered a crowd to disperse, they would become “co-responsible” for whatever happens next. For minors, their parents would have to pay the actions of their children. And to make sure money can be extracted from the rebellious poor, the law allows authorities to garnish money directly from potential housing benefits and family allowances. In short, this law once again targets low-income individuals and families perceived as threats to the ruling order, as well as anyone who would dare to defy authority.




Beyond these repressive measures, the government also scrambled to find “solutions”—i.e., distractions—to end the crisis. During his speech, Lecornu also insisted that the government, via the Ministry of Education, had implemented tools for high school students to take part in some sort of national survey where they can express their frustrations and make requests to improve the educational system. Such strategy of watered-down participatory democracy was also used during the Yellow Vest movement to divide demonstrators and weaken their collective force. First, the French government represses students in cold blood; then it asks them for “constructive” dialogue.




Lecornu explained that by the end of the month, the government would study and work to address all the demands received by students via their official platforms to provide concrete solutions to the current crisis in the educational system. He also promised to improve “ParcourSup,” the online platform with which students list their “wishes” and apply to different post-secondary education options. He also announced that until the end of the week, each high school has been asked by the Ministry of Education to cancel half a day of classes in order to create some space and time for “a period of internal democracy” during which students and teachers could exchange about what should be changed within the school. This isn’t the first time that 

the language of “democracy”

 has been used as a tool for counterinsurgency.




Similarly, on October 8 Education Minister Édouard Geffray made a new promise to 

provide

 3000 extra teachers, while welcoming student unions and organizations to contribute their views on the current situation in hopes of reaching a political agreement to end the demonstrations as soon as possible. These promises and calls for dialogue show the Macron government’s strategy to pacify the situation by partially answering some of the main demands made by the student movement—while ratcheting up repression in the streets to maintain power on their own terms.




National media have reported that tens of thousands of demands were already made by students through these official platforms. Nonetheless, it seems to us that, so far, doing so has not stopped them from continuing to be present in the streets. Even students who may participate in such official channels recognize that their collective power to disrupt the status quo, not the government’s pacifying gestures, remains the source of their genuine power and voice.




So far, the student movement has resisted cooptation by political opportunists and trade unions. However, its success and widespread public support render it a tempting target for those who would attempt to control it or hitch it to other agendas. University student unions and their spokespeople form part of the movement, and some leftist politicians and their followers actively support it. However, none of them have yet been able to speak on behalf of all its participants, nor to control the diversity of tactics that have flourished within it.




Finally, the existing solidarity within the ranks of students is admirable. As we 

reported previously

, teenagers face vastly different realities depending on the geographical areas where they live and study. The claim of the French school system to promote equal opportunity and reward merit rather than class and geographic background is simply a lie, in the face of the structural inequalities that flourish within capitalism and the educational system designed to reinforce it. Nevertheless, while high-school students in the suburbs were facing violent repression from police forces, students from wealthier districts and prestigious universities joined the struggle by blocking or occupying their schools in solidarity. Numerous students explained that although they are well aware that they do not experience the same difficulties as their counterparts living in the 

banlieues

, they could not remain passive in the face of such police violence and injustice against their counterparts.




Students blocking the Hélène-Boucher high school. The sign reads: “Fewer cops, more money.” (Paris, October 6, 2026)




Onward Together Against Their World




Following another intense week of actions and protests, the Ministry of Justice 

announced

 on Friday, October 9 that since the beginning of the movement, more than 6800 people have been taken into custody, 86% of whom are minors. So far, 21 individuals have been held in jail while awaiting trial.




At the eve of a new weekend, the government continued to promote the narrative that the movement was declining and the situation was progressively coming back under control, trumpeting the decreasing number of blocked high schools as evidence. But despite the mainstream media’s faithful adherence to this story, students remained unsatisfied by the government’s response and determined not to give up the fight. Far from feeling defeated, they issued a new call to take to the streets on Tuesday, October 13.




Act V: October 13, 2026




As the next day of action dawned, blockades and clashes with law enforcement forced the closure of about 200 high schools. Over the previous days, that number had held steady, showing that a significant core of high school students remained willing to fight for what they think is right.




But what changed dramatically on this day compared to the previous acts is that a large number of universities decided to join the movement all at once. Around noon, the organization 

Union étudiante

 announced to the media that 90% of the seventy French universities were blocked or completely closed. This massive involvement of university students during the fifth act of the student unrest would prove to be a critical development.




The sign reads: “High-school students maimed, shot in the eye, drowned, or toothless. University students outraged.” (Rennes, October 6, 2026)




As the movement expanded and gained in strength, the counterrevolutionary backlash against it from both the government and the grassroots extreme right increased in turn. The growing number of blockades at universities over these days led to a surge in fascist attacks intended to intimidate protesters in cities such as Paris and Lille.




As usual, the first marches throughout France took place in the morning. In Paris, the official demonstration was announced for 2:00 pm. This time, the itinerary validated by authorities changed from the classic Place de la République to La Nation. Demonstrators would be storming the southern and western parts of the city, departing from Place d’Italie and reaching Invalides, not far from the Ministry of Education and Matignon, the official residence of the Prime Minister. This route evoked sweet memories from another famous student movement that took place in France 

20 years ago

, during which intense riots took place once demonstrators reached Invalides. Another unofficial call went out summoning protestors to meet in front of City Hall. This unauthorized procession was finally granted the right to walk through the streets of Paris to reach its destination not far from the other demonstration.




On the afternoon of the 13th, police forces changed their tactics and drew up very close to the demonstrators, moving at the front of the procession. Before participants could join the march, they were subject to search by the police. Officers attempted to confiscate as many anti-police signs as possible. However, this strategy to muzzle public opinion against the police’s violent behavior proved unsuccessful, as thousands of protesters took pleasure in chanting the classic anti-police slogans in unison during the march.




As demonstrators approached their final destination, tensions with law enforcement escalated. Near Invalides, some motivated protesters attempted to continue their afternoon march towards Matignon, but were quickly stopped and pushed back by lines of police near Place Vauban.




It was here that intense confrontations unfolded over the next several hours. Police deployed water cannons and blanketed the square with tear gas in order to disperse the crowd. What demonstrators didn’t know yet was that other police units had surrounded them and stood ready to kettle them if needed in order to arrest specific individuals. During the clashes, rioters set a BMW SUV on fire and looted a nearby wine store.




Street confrontations at 

Place Vauban

 (Paris, October 13, 2026)




Later that night, the government stated that 161,500 people demonstrated during the fifth act of the student movement, while the student unions claimed a total turnout of 480,000. Officials estimated 41,500 demonstrators in Paris. Further demonstrations took place in Nantes, Lens, Strasbourg, Bordeaux, Marseille and Lyon, where some confrontations with police forces and property destruction took place towards the end of the march.




By the end of the day, arrest figures had shot up further. 7950 individuals had been taken into police custody since the beginning of the student protests, 85% of whom were minors. To date, 2735 criminal cases had been filed, 2190 of which involved minors, and 26 individuals were placed in pretrial detention, including 9 minors.




Looking Forward: Will the Unrest Survive the Holidays?




As the first school holidays of the year approached, many students wondered whether their month-long mobilization would survive the two-week break from classes. Their worries were understandable; it is well known that holidays have often taken the wind out of the sails of many social movements, in France and beyond.




This is why, for days, high-school students have continuously called to take the street on Saturday, October 17, 2026. This call, massively shared online for weeks, suggests a resurgence of 

the Yellow Vest movement

 that launched in 2018. Rebellious high schoolers hoped that university students, Yellow Vesters, and other angry protesters would be able to merge with the movement to expand this social and political unrest in new directions.




We haven’t been defeated yet. (Paris, October 13, 2026)




Meanwhile, the government continued to find itself in a bind over the 

crisis

, despite its pathetic attempts to defuse the uproar through dialogue with student unions and organizations. After weeks of insisting that the movement was losing steam, now they are acknowledging that the level of militancy and determination coming from protesters has progressively increased over the previous days of action. They feared the potential outcome of the October 17 demonstrations—and as we have seen, their fears were justified.




With the fateful date approaching and tension building, important questions remained. Will other demographics decide to join the movement by also revolting against the government and their current living conditions, as authorities fear? Will we live up to the expectations of high school students and the courageous precedent they have set? Will we be able to unleash hell?




Will the student movement be able to unleash hell? (Paris, October 6, 2026).

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The “enemy” isn’t in the streets. It’s what sends you there
content:
by Leonardo Caffo




from 

The Anarchist Library




From France to Albania, from Belgium to Turin, the protests of these days stage a clash between metaphors. Young people (the people) and police officers (the State), equally precarious, face each other as if the other were the enemy. But the enemy stopped living where we look for it long ago. And that is precisely where it organizes the anger, makes it visible and summons it into the street.




Let me say this right away, to leave no room for misunderstanding: the young people who have been filling the streets of Europe in recent weeks have every right to do so. This is not a rhetorical concession, one of those premises you write only to take back three lines later. They have reasons to spare: schools falling apart, overcrowded classrooms, a future shrinking like a room whose walls someone moves at night while we sleep. Anyone who dismisses them as vandals, as spoiled children of a prosperity they no longer know, or as puppets of some hidden director, has understood nothing. Or pretends not to understand, which is worse. But precisely because they are right, and precisely because their distress is real, it is worth asking the question nobody seems willing to ask these weeks. Not because it is difficult, but because it is uncomfortable for everyone: for governments, for movements, for newspapers, for commentators. The question is simple. Against whom are they protesting? In favor of what?




There is no point asking against 

what

. The what is clear, even too clear: the cuts, the cost of living, the decrees, the war that swallows resources, the idea that school should serve the labor market rather than people, impossible rents. But where does the power that produces all this live, if it lives anywhere at all? Because a protest without an addressee is not an absence of politics: it is a politics someone else is doing in your place, using your body, your time, your anger.







I. The scene: a Europe that always ends up in the same frame




Let us look at the images before interpreting them. In France the mobilization began in September in Brittany, in the schools, against staff shortages and the decay of public education, and spread across the whole country. On October 6, according to the Interior Ministry, more than 250,000 people were in the streets; according to the organizers, almost twice that. The toll of weeks of protest runs to thousands of arrests and hundreds injured, among students, teachers and officers. In Lens a fifteen-year-old boy lost a hand after coming into contact with a police grenade. In Brussels, on October 9, unions striking against budget cuts were joined by hundreds of students inspired by what was happening in France. A few dozen masked protesters threw stones at the police; the police responded with tear gas and water cannons; twenty-one people were detained, thirteen of them minors. In Albania, the student protest outside the Ministry of Education on October 13 turned within hours into a revolt against the Rama government: the Ministry of Justice in flames, attacks on public buildings, banks and businesses, 89 injured, 61 of them officers.




And then Italy. On October 16 thousands of students marched in every city against the school decree, the cap on foreign pupils in classrooms, the 4+2 model for technical institutes, the cost of living, military spending. In Milan, a river of second-generation young people, born here or arrived as children, forming a shield against those who would like to count them. In Rome, bottles and firecrackers outside the ministry. In Bologna, shields in front of the station. In Turin, stones against officers, water cannons against students, and in between some teachers who placed themselves between the two lines, as their French colleagues had done a few days earlier. You don’t need to be a sociologist to notice that the causes are different, and so are the contexts, and yet the final frame is always the same. A kid in a hood facing a kid in a helmet. The protest is born against something enormous and undefined, a social model, a stolen future, a politics that does not listen. And it ends, with almost mechanical regularity, in hand-to-hand combat between two people who have never met and have no personal reason to hate each other.




This frame is the real political subject under discussion today. Not because the clash is the heart of the matter: on the contrary, I argue that it is peripheral. But because that frame is a symptom, in the precise sense the word has in psychoanalysis: a compromise formation that shows and hides at the same time. It shows that there is a conflict. It hides who is really party to it. And the media, who love that frame because it brings in viewers, only amplify its function as a screen. Even the mayor of Turin said so, with unexpected lucidity: there are those who use those images to talk only about the clashes, leaving the problems the young people raise in the background.




II. Two metaphors facing each other in a mirror




Let us return to those two bodies. The student in the street is a metaphor: he stands for a generation whose future has been taken away, for a school turned into the antechamber of employment, for an existence that discovers itself precarious before it has even begun. But the police officer is a metaphor too. In fact, if you look closely, he embodies it even better. He is often young as well, almost always from the peripheries and the South, poorly paid for a hellish job that asks him to stand for hours under a hail of bottles to defend a ministry whose minister he will never meet. He too has watched his future shrink; he too is the product of a social model that offers a uniform as the only possible stability. The difference between the two is not one of class. It is one of position: one has been put in front, the other behind a shield.




Pier Paolo Pasolini understood this in 1968 when, after the clashes at Valle Giulia, he wrote that his sympathies lay with the police officers, sons of the poor, and not with the students, children of the bourgeoisie. It was a heresy, and he was treated as a reactionary (and hardly anyone has ever read how that line continues, something Ascanio Celestini does very well in his new book on Pasolini). But Pasolini’s gesture was not a defense of the police: it was an attempt to shift the gaze from the choreography to the structure, to remind us that within that clash stood bodies socially closer than the flags let on. Today that intuition has become even truer, and at the same time more tragic. Truer, because the social distance between the student and the officer has narrowed further: the kids in the streets of Milan are the children of workers, migrants, precarious laborers. More tragic, because in the meantime the master those officers once shielded has disappeared. In 1968 behind the cordon there was still the State, there was the bourgeoisie, there was an enemy with an address. Today behind the cordon there is a palace often empty of real power.




Hegel, in the 

Phenomenology of Spirit

, describes the struggle for recognition as the moment when two self-consciousnesses confront each other at the risk of their lives, and from which the relationship between master and servant arises. The decisive point, the one Alexandre Kojève would make famous in his Paris lectures, is that the struggle only makes sense if there is a master by whom to be recognized. But what happens when the struggle takes place between two servants? When both contenders seek recognition from a third party who is not present, and who has no interest in recognizing anyone? The dialectic jams. There is no synthesis, no overcoming, no history. There is only repetition: the same scene, every week, in a different city.




René Girard gave this mechanism a name. In 

Violence and the Sacred

 and then in 

The Scapegoat

, Girard shows how communities in crisis discharge accumulated violence onto a substitute victim, who is not the cause of the crisis but becomes its symbol. The sacrifice solves nothing, but it temporarily restores order: the violence is discharged, the tension drops, everything can start again as before. The street clash works exactly like this, and it works in both directions. For the student, the police officer is the scapegoat of the system: striking him is symbolically striking power. For the State, and for the public reading the next day’s papers, the violent student is the scapegoat of disorder: punishing him reaffirms order. Each sacrifices the other. No one touches the cause.




That is why I speak of a clash between metaphors. Not to diminish the pain, which is all too real: the hand lost in Lens is no figure of speech, nor are the 61 officers injured in Tirana. But because what confronts itself in those streets is not the subjects of the conflict but their representations. Two figures of distress set against each other, each convinced the other is the obstacle. And while they stare into each other’s eyes, neither looks up from the screen.




III. Power has changed address




If we look up, what do we see? We see that what is at stake in the streets of Paris, Tirana, Brussels, Madrid and Turin is no longer, or no longer only, a matter of States. Local governments, with their budgets and decrees, are the visible target: the one you can name in a slogan, the one outside whose ministry a march can stop. But the organization of society that produces the distress now has little to do with ministries. Governments administer ever-narrower margins within constraints decided elsewhere: by the financial markets that rate the debt, by the platforms that control the infrastructure of information, by the large corporations that decide where to move capital, production, labor.




Michel Foucault, back in the 1970s, taught us to distrust the idea that power resides in a place. Power, he wrote, is not a thing one possesses; it is a network of relations running through bodies, institutions, forms of knowledge. It is not at the top of the pyramid; it is everywhere. But Foucault was still thinking of disciplinary institutions: the school, the barracks, the factory, the prison. Closed places, with walls and timetables, where power shaped individuals. Gilles Deleuze, in a short 1990 text that now reads like a prophecy, the 

Postscript on the Societies of Control

, had already announced the end of that model. Disciplinary societies, he said, are giving way to societies of control, in which power no longer confines but modulates, no longer watches within an enclosure but follows everywhere, continuously and without boundaries. Man, Deleuze observed, is no longer man enclosed but man in debt. And he added a detail that sounds chilling today: in the society of control, school would be replaced by lifelong training, and the corporation would take the factory’s place as the soul of the system. Reread that text thinking of the 4+2 model, of work-study schemes, of school as one segment in a human-capital supply chain, and you realize that this autumn’s students are protesting precisely against what Deleuze described. But they do so with the tools of another era: the march, the occupation, the siege of the ministry. Tools designed for a power that had a center, a palace, a door to break down. Control power, by contrast, has no doors. You cannot besiege it, because it is nowhere.




Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri (who knows how pleased he would have been today), in 

Empire

, described this form of sovereignty as a decentered and deterritorializing apparatus, with no territorial center and no fixed boundaries. One can argue at length about their political conclusions, but the diagnosis stands: sovereignty no longer coincides with the nation-state. Power has evaporated into the global space of flows, while politics has remained local. Power without politics on one side, politics without power on the other. In between, the streets. And here we understand why the young people’s anger, even when it finds a precise target, such as the Italian decree or the Rama government, always ends up seeming a little disproportionate, a little out of focus. Not because it is unjustified, but because the addressee is not equal to the message. A minister is being asked to give back a future it is not in his power to give back. A national government is being asked to reverse processes that national governments have, for decades, merely managed. The street shouts at the palace, but the palace is only the switchboard of a power that answers from another number. The ministry, in this scene, is as much a metaphor as the student and the police officer: it is the visible face of decisions it does not make.




IV. The paradox of the medium: what moves you is what you are fighting




There is, however, something deeper, and more disturbing, than the simple evaporation of power upward. And it is the real news of this autumn, the news no newscast will report. The protests are organized on the very platforms that embody the power they protest against. The chats where the meeting point is decided, the social networks that call for mobilization, the algorithms that circulate videos of the clashes: these are all private infrastructures, owned by a few corporations, fueled by an economic model that lives on attention, data, conflict. What moves the young people and what they would like to fight coincide. The medium of the revolt is its target.




Marshall McLuhan put it in a phrase that has become a cliché and that, for this very reason, no one takes seriously anymore: the medium is the message. What matters is not only what is said, but through what it is said, because the medium alters the very form of experience. A protest organized on a platform is not the same as a protest organized in an assembly. It inherits the platform’s grammar: speed, fragmentation, the hunt for the image, polarization. Above all it inherits its economic logic. Every shared video of clashes is monetized attention. Every call to mobilize is a data point. Every expression of rage online is engagement. The platform is not neutral toward the conflict: it lives off it. And it has every interest in the conflict taking its most spectacular form, namely physical confrontation, because that is what generates the most views.




It is a telling detail that in France a fact-checking organization identified fake videos circulated to inflate the chaos and violence of the protests. It does not matter here who produced them. What matters is that the ecosystem rewards them. Guy Debord, in 

The Society of the Spectacle

, wrote that the spectacle is not a collection of images but a social relationship between people mediated by images. And there it is: today’s street is exactly that. A social relationship, the one between the student and the police officer, entirely mediated by the images that will be drawn from it. People take to the streets partly to be seen, and they are seen only if the clash happens. The spectacle has absorbed the contestation of the spectacle, as Debord feared and as the Situationists, in the end, could not prevent.




Byung-Chul Han added a decisive piece. In 

Psychopolitics

 he observes that contemporary power does not repress freedom; it exploits it. It does not force us to be silent; it encourages us to speak, to express ourselves, to share. It is a seductive power, working through our desire rather than against it. That is why, Han says, it is so hard to rebel: because rebellion itself becomes a form of participation in the system. Shoshana Zuboff, in 

The Age of Surveillance Capitalism

, gave this mechanism a precise economic anatomy: human experience turned into free raw material, extracted, analyzed and resold as behavioral prediction. The anger of a generation is an extraordinary mine of behavioral data. And it is extracted as it is being expressed.




The result is a paradox reminiscent of the knot in certain ancient myths, where the hero flees his fate and, by fleeing, fulfills it. The young people are fighting a model of society governed by financial and digital flows, using those very flows as their only means of organization. This is not a fault, not naivety: it is the condition of anyone living today. There is no available outside, no uncontaminated place from which to organize resistance. But precisely for this reason it should be named. Because as long as it goes unnamed, that paradox works in silence, and it always works in the same direction: it turns protest into content, content into clashes, clashes into ratings. And power, the real one, thanks you for your cooperation.




V. Simulacra of struggle




All this leads to a conclusion that must be stated carefully, because it is easy to misread. This autumn’s struggles risk becoming simulacra. Not in the sense that they are fake: the pain is real, the reasons are real, the bruises are real. But in the precise sense Jean Baudrillard gave the word. In 

Simulacra and Simulation

 Baudrillard describes a sequence: first the image reflects a reality, then it masks it, then it masks its absence, and finally it bears no relation to any reality whatsoever and is its own pure simulacrum. The street clash passes through every one of these phases. At first it represents a real conflict, between a generation and a social model. Then it masks it, because it replaces it with another conflict, between students and police. Then it masks its absence, because the real adversary is not present and the scene serves to make us believe it is. Finally it becomes autonomous: people take to the streets for the clash, the clash produces images, the images produce the next protest.




Baudrillard wrote a provocative book titled 

The Gulf War Did Not Take Place

. Obviously he did not deny the bombs and the dead. He argued that what the Western public had seen was not a war but its televised simulation, an event built to be watched. One could write an equally provocative book today: the revolt is not taking place. Not because there are no people in the streets, but because the event we call revolt is increasingly its own representation, a coded sequence of gestures, slogans, images and reactions everyone knows in advance. The minister will say the violence is unacceptable; the opposition will say the young people must be listened to; the police union will demand more protection; the papers will headline the clashes. And the next day nothing structural will have changed.




Mark Fisher, in 

Capitalist Realism

, described the condition of a generation for whom it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism. Fisher’s point was not that capitalism was invincible, but that it had colonized the imagination to the point of making any alternative unthinkable. Protest too, in this picture, is precoded: there is a space set aside for dissent, a format, a genre, with its own rules and outcomes. Fisher spoke of gestural anti-capitalism: critique of the system expressed as style, as pose, without touching the mechanisms. I am not saying the young people of Turin or Paris are posing. I am saying the system they move within has already anticipated their anger and prepared a stage for it.




The enormous political problem today is that the individual can no longer represent to himself the totality of the system he lives in. Global capitalism is too vast, too abstract, too distributed for anyone to draw its map and locate themselves within it. Without that map, political action is blind: you strike what you see, not what matters. The police officer is visible. The ministry is visible. The capital flow that decided a school’s closure, the algorithm that decided which protest to show and which not, the investment fund that owns the platform on which the protest was called: these cannot be seen. And what cannot be seen cannot be fought. This is the heart of the simulacrum: the struggle takes place between sections of the population equally in distress, while the distress itself is produced elsewhere. The student who will never have a pension and the officer who barely makes it to the end of the month. The precarious teacher who steps in to protect his pupils and the shopkeeper whose window is smashed. The second-generation immigrant marching against the cap on foreigners and the pensioner watching him fearfully from the window. All in difficulty, all convinced they have the problem in front of them. None of them truly in a position to solve it.




VI. Infiltrators, clashes, legitimacy: the wrong questions




I already know what objections will come, because they are the same ones repeated every hot autumn. There are infiltrators, professional troublemakers, those who in Turin seemed a little too old to be students. According to the Albanian police, of the dozens detained after the Tirana clashes only a few were students. The police, on the other side, use disproportionate force, and human rights organizations have been denouncing it in France for weeks. Burning a ministry is not legitimate; or it is, if the ministry is deaf. Throwing a stone is violence; or it is the response to a greater, structural, invisible violence.




These are serious discussions, and I do not intend to dismiss them. Twentieth-century political philosophy left us refined tools for tackling them. Walter Benjamin, in his 

Critique of Violence

, distinguished between law-making and law-preserving violence, and showed how every legal order is born of a violence it then forgets. Hannah Arendt, in 

On Violence

, argued the opposite: that violence and power are opposites; where power is real, that is, grounded in consent and acting in concert, violence is unnecessary; violence appears where power is waning, and it can destroy power but never create it. Frantz Fanon, in 

The Wretched of the Earth

, saw in the violence of the colonized a moment of detoxification, a way of reclaiming a denied subjectivity. These are three incompatible positions, and each illuminates something.




But it is Arendt who gives us the key to understanding why these questions are secondary today. If violence appears where power is waning, then the violence in these streets is the sign of a power vacuum. Not of an excess of state power, as those throwing stones believe. Not of an excess of youthful disorder, as those repressing them believe. But of a vacuum: real power, the power that decides, is not present, and the two bodies left in the street collide because they have nothing else to hit. Street violence is the shape politics takes when politics no longer has an interlocutor.




That is why the debate over who is infiltrating, over how far it is acceptable to make use of a mobilization that destroys everything, over what the acceptable threshold of force might be, is a debate about the choreography, not the music. Every hour spent establishing who threw the first stone is an hour not spent talking about where the money missing from schools ends up. Every editorial on student violence, or on police brutality, is one editorial fewer on who owns the infrastructures through which we think, on what form of life we are accepting without ever having chosen it. I am not saying those questions should not be asked. I am saying they are the questions the system prefers us to ask, because they keep us busy arguing about the perimeter while the center remains intact.




There is, indeed, a suspicion worth formulating, even if it cannot be proven. Street violence benefits everyone except those who suffer it. It benefits governments, which can shift the conversation from the reasons for the protest to security. It benefits the most radical groups, which gain visibility. It benefits the media, which gain viewers. It benefits the platforms, which gain traffic. It does not benefit the students, who see their reasons buried under the images. It does not benefit the police officers, who risk their bodies for a miserable salary. An economy of violence in which the gains are distributed at the top and the costs at the bottom: is that not the most precise definition of the system being protested against?




VII. The enemy exists, and it is shared




Carl Schmitt identified the distinction between friend and enemy as the very criterion of the political. To do politics, for Schmitt, means being able to name the enemy. It is a dangerous thesis, one that has justified horrors, and I do not propose it as a model. But it contains a truth that today’s streets make evident by contrast: whoever cannot name their enemy does not do politics, they endure it. And whoever gets the enemy wrong is doing someone else’s politics. The student who sees the police officer as the enemy, and the police officer who sees the student as the enemy, are both applying Schmitt’s criterion in the worst possible way: they have identified their own kind as the enemy.




The enemy exists. It is shared: shared by students and police officers, by the teachers who step in between and the parents watching the news, by the second-generation kids of Milan and the pensioners who fear them. It is an organization of society founded on extraction: of value from labor, of data from lives, of attention from emotions, of future from the generations to come. It has no face, because it is made of flows. It has no headquarters, because it is distributed. It has no name, because every name we give it, finance, platforms, corporations, capital, captures only one aspect. But it has precise, measurable effects that the young people in the streets know very well: collapsing schools, impossible rents, fixed-term contracts, a climate in collapse. The enemy, then, is not in those streets. It is what sends you into those streets. It is what organizes your anger, lays it out, makes it go viral, turns it into content and then channels it into the one outlet that costs it nothing: having you tear each other apart. While, outside the frame, the world crumbles, work dissolves, school becomes a supply chain, and those who profit from all this have never needed to put on a helmet or a balaclava.




This is not an invitation to stay home. That would be the most convenient advice for the system I have described, and the most unjust toward young people who are right. It is an invitation to protest better. To turn the street from a stage into a place of thought: assemblies, inquiries, maps of power drawn together. To seek unexpected alliances, even with those on the other side of the shield, who have a union, a salary and a child attending the same crumbling school. To hold governments to account, of course, but also those above them: the platforms, the funds, the supranational institutions that decide without ever setting foot in the street. And not to forget that the phone you use to organize the next march also belongs to someone: try disconnecting all at once, all of you, stop posting and go back somewhere else, and see how suddenly everything would collapse.

title: Giorgio Agamben: Knowledge and knowability
content:
Titian, 

Nymph and Shepherd

, 1570




Time and again, we must question the primacy of knowledge in our culture, and ask ourselves whether, in truth – in the words that open Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* – what human beings desire above all else is to know. If we restore to “truth” its etymological meaning of “non-concealment” (a-letheia), then what is at stake in that truth is not knowledge itself, but knowability—the openness from which only something like knowledge becomes possible. If we call the manifest being, the self-giving and the appearing of each thing, a “face”, then truth lies in that original openness; it is the memory of the faces of things and not their reduction to objects of knowledge and science. And since we experience pleasure and fall in love with appearances and faces, any form of knowledge that seeks to dispense with them cannot in any way contribute to our happiness. If art and philosophy still hold our interest, it is because they concern themselves not with knowledge, but with the knowability of things and people. A culture such as the one in which we live, which forgets faces and pursues knowledge at all costs, can therefore only end—as is evident today—in the blind and destructive domination of the world by a science that has been transformed into the most intolerant of religions.

title: Giorgio Agamben: A general demobilisation
content:
“The Worker” by Vladimir Serov, 1964







In 1932, Ernst Jünger published 

Der Arbeiter

 [

The Worker

], a work in which this new figure of humanity pointed to the new world order. The centrality of work corresponds to the dominance of technology. Expanding on concepts he had expressed in his book of two years prior, 

Total Mobilization

, Jünger writes: “Technology is the way in which the worker form mobilises the world.” This diagnosis, which revisited Marx’s analyses from an entirely different perspective, exerted considerable influence on both the right and the left of the political spectrum.




It is therefore all the more surprising that this decisive figure of the era has disappeared for some decades now. Technology continues to govern the world and has certainly increased its power everywhere, but it is no longer “the way in which the worker form mobilises the world.” On the contrary, in the form of artificial intelligence, it seems to imply rather the decline of the centrality of work that Jünger had in mind. Instead of the servitude linked to exploitation and mobilisation, technology, by progressively blurring the identities of social classes and estates, seems today to be heading towards an unprecedented form of subjugation through a kind of general demobilisation.
